{{Infobox religious building | name = Kagoshima-jingū
鹿児島神宮 | image = Kagoshimajingu Chokushiden.JPG | caption = Imperial Messenger's Hall (ICP) {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Kagoshima Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|31|45|13.37|N|130|44|16.3|E|region:JP-46|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kagoshima-jingū | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Hachiman]] | deity = [[Hoori]]
[[Toyotama-hime]]
[[Emperor Chūai]]
[[Emperor Ōjin]]
[[Empress Jingū]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 2496, Hayato-chō Uchi, Kirishima-shi, Kagoshima-ken 899-5116 | website = | architecture_style = [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''irimoya-zukuri'']] | festival = August 15 (lunar) | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Kagoshima Shrine'''|鹿児島神宮|''Kagoshima-jingū''}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the [[Hayato, Kagoshima|Hayatomachi-uchi]] neighborhood of the city of [[Kirishima, Kagoshima|Kirishima]], [[Kagoshima prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Ōsumi Province]]. The main festival of the shrine are held annually on August 15 by the [[lunar calendar]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Historically it was also known by the names {{nihongo| '''Ōsumi Shō-Hachiman-gū''' |大隅正八幡宮||}} and {{nihongo| '''Kokubu Hachiman-gū'''|国分八幡宮||}}. The shrine precincts was designated as a [[Historic Sites of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/280010|title= 大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} == Enshrined ''Kami'' == The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kagoshima-jingū are:{{Cite web |title=由緒について - 鹿児島神宮 |url=https://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=kagoshima-jingu.jp}} ; Main shrine * {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]]'''|天津日高彦火火出見尊|}}, son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyotama-hime]]'''| 豊玉比売命|}}, wife of Hoori, paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu ; Subsidiary shrines * [[Emperor Chūai]] (帯中比子尊) * [[Empress Jingū]] (息長帯比売命) - Wife of Emperor Chūai. * [[Emperor Ōjin]] (品陀和気尊) * [[Nakatsuhime]] (中比売命) - Wife of Emperor Ōjin. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, the Kagoshima Jingū during the [[Age of the Gods]], as Takachiho Palace, the residence of [[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] (彦火火出見尊), the third and youngest son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] and ancestor of [[Emperor Jimmu]]. It was moved to its current location in 708, and Setsusha Sekitai-gu (Ishitai Shrine) is currently located on the former site. Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. Kagoshima-jingu, honden.jpg|Honden (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Auxiliary Auxiliary-Shrine Shisyo-jinja 001.jpg|Shisho Jinja (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Decoration of Shrine Buildings 001.jpg|Decoration on Chokushi-den (ICP) ===National Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿|Main Shrine}}, {{nihongo|'''Chokushi-den'''|勅使殿|Imperial Messenger Hall}}, and {{nihongo|'''Sessha Shisho Jinja Honden'''|摂社四所神社本殿|Sub-shrine Shisho Jinja Main Shrine}}, constructed in 1755 by Shimazu Shigetoshi and completed by Shimazu Shigehide. Designated [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]] in 2022{{Cite web |last=霧島市 |title=国宝・重要文化財(建造物)の指定について |url=http://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kokuhoukettei.html |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=霧島市 |language=ja}} ==See also== *[[List of Historic Sites of Japan (Kagoshima)]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category|Kagoshima-jingu|Kagoshima Shrine}} * {{OSM|n|4459864389}} {{Shinto shrine}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[en:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:Shikinai Taisha]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:History of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Ōsumi Province]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[Category:Kirishima, Kagoshima]] [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:pages and categories from Wikipedia]] [[Category:confused probably misplaced articles linked from page Torinoichi probably under wrong names recheck that page and its outlinks later]] [[Category:kk]] [[Category:attempting to force efresh]] [[Category:bump1-19]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[en:Kagoshima Shrine]]

Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. Kagoshima-jingu, honden.jpg|Honden (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Auxiliary Auxiliary-Shrine Shisyo-jinja 001.jpg|Shisho Jinja (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Decoration of Shrine Buildings 001.jpg|Decoration on Chokushi-den (ICP) ===National Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿|Main Shrine}}, {{nihongo|'''Chokushi-den'''|勅使殿|Imperial Messenger Hall}}, and {{nihongo|'''Sessha Shisho Jinja Honden'''|摂社四所神社本殿|Sub-shrine Shisho Jinja Main Shrine}}, constructed in 1755 by Shimazu Shigetoshi and completed by Shimazu Shigehide. Designated [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]] in 2022{{Cite web |last=霧島市 |title=国宝・重要文化財(建造物)の指定について |url=http://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kokuhoukettei.html |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=霧島市 |language=ja}} ==See also== *[[List of Historic Sites of Japan (Kagoshima)]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category|Kagoshima-jingu|Kagoshima Shrine}} * {{OSM|n|4459864389}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]][[en:Kagoshima Jingu]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[en:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:Shikinai Taisha]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:History of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Ōsumi Province]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[Category:Kirishima, Kagoshima]] [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:pages and categories from Wikipedia]] [[Category:confused probably misplaced articles linked from page Torinoichi probably under wrong names recheck that page and its outlinks later]] [[Category:kk]] [[Category:attempting to force efresh]] [[Category:bump1-19]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]][[Category:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[en:Kagoshima Shrine]]

Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. [[Toyotama-hime]]
[[Emperor Chūai]]
[[Emperor Ōjin]]
[[Empress Jingū]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 2496, Hayato-chō Uchi, Kirishima-shi, Kagoshima-ken 899-5116 | website = | architecture_style = [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''irimoya-zukuri'']] | festival = August 15 (lunar) | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Kagoshima Shrine'''|鹿児島神宮|''Kagoshima-jingū''}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the [[Hayato, Kagoshima|Hayatomachi-uchi]] neighborhood of the city of [[Kirishima, Kagoshima|Kirishima]], [[Kagoshima prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Ōsumi Province]]. The main festival of the shrine are held annually on August 15 by the [[lunar calendar]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Historically it was also known by the names {{nihongo| '''Ōsumi Shō-Hachiman-gū''' |大隅正八幡宮||}} and {{nihongo| '''Kokubu Hachiman-gū'''|国分八幡宮||}}. The shrine precincts was designated as a [[Historic Sites of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/280010|title= 大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} == Enshrined ''Kami'' == The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kagoshima-jingū are:{{Cite web |title=由緒について - 鹿児島神宮 |url=https://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=kagoshima-jingu.jp}} ; Main shrine * {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]]'''|天津日高彦火火出見尊|}}, son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyotama-hime]]'''| 豊玉比売命|}}, wife of Hoori, paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu ; Subsidiary shrines * [[Emperor Chūai]] (帯中比子尊) * [[Empress Jingū]] (息長帯比売命) - Wife of Emperor Chūai. * [[Emperor Ōjin]] (品陀和気尊) * [[Nakatsuhime]] (中比売命) - Wife of Emperor Ōjin. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, the Kagoshima Jingū during the [[Age of the Gods]], as Takachiho Palace, the residence of [[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] (彦火火出見尊), the third and youngest son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] and ancestor of [[Emperor Jimmu]]. It was moved to its current location in 708, and Setsusha Sekitai-gu (Ishitai Shrine) is currently located on the former site. Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. Designated [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]] in 2022{{Cite web |last=霧島市 |title=国宝・重要文化財(建造物)の指定について |url=http://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kokuhoukettei.html |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=霧島市 |language=ja}} ==See also== *[[List of Historic Sites of Japan (Kagoshima)]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category|Kagoshima-jingu|Kagoshima Shrine}} * {{OSM|n|4459864389}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]][[en:Kagoshima Jingu]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[en:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:Shikinai Taisha]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:History of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Ōsumi Province]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[Category:Kirishima, Kagoshima]] [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 7]] [[Category:confused probably misplaced articles linked from page Torinoichi probably under wrong names recheck that page and its outlinks later]] [[Category:kk]] [[Category:attempting to force efresh]] [[Category:bump1-19]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]][[Category:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:refreshing imports]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]][[Category:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[en:Kagoshima Shrine]]

The main festival of the shrine are held annually on August 15 by the [[lunar calendar]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Historically it was also known by the names {{nihongo| '''Ōsumi Shō-Hachiman-gū''' |大隅正八幡宮||}} and {{nihongo| '''Kokubu Hachiman-gū'''|国分八幡宮||}}. The shrine precincts was designated as a [[Historic Sites of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/280010|title= 大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} == Enshrined ''Kami'' == The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kagoshima-jingū are:{{Cite web |title=由緒について - 鹿児島神宮 |url=https://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=kagoshima-jingu.jp}} ; Main shrine * {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]]'''|天津日高彦火火出見尊|}}, son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyotama-hime]]'''| 豊玉比売命|}}, wife of Hoori, paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu ; Subsidiary shrines * [[Emperor Chūai]] (帯中比子尊) * [[Empress Jingū]] (息長帯比売命) - Wife of Emperor Chūai. * [[Emperor Ōjin]] (品陀和気尊) * [[Nakatsuhime]] (中比売命) - Wife of Emperor Ōjin. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, the Kagoshima Jingū during the [[Age of the Gods]], as Takachiho Palace, the residence of [[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] (彦火火出見尊), the third and youngest son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] and ancestor of [[Emperor Jimmu]]. It was moved to its current location in 708, and Setsusha Sekitai-gu (Ishitai Shrine) is currently located on the former site. Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. Kagoshima-jingu, honden.jpg|Honden (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Auxiliary Auxiliary-Shrine Shisyo-jinja 001.jpg|Shisho Jinja (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Decoration of Shrine Buildings 001.jpg|Decoration on Chokushi-den (ICP) ===National Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿|Main Shrine}}, {{nihongo|'''Chokushi-den'''|勅使殿|Imperial Messenger Hall}}, and {{nihongo|'''Sessha Shisho Jinja Honden'''|摂社四所神社本殿|Sub-shrine Shisho Jinja Main Shrine}}, constructed in 1755 by Shimazu Shigetoshi and completed by Shimazu Shigehide. Designated [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]] in 2022{{Cite web |last=霧島市 |title=国宝・重要文化財(建造物)の指定について |url=http://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kokuhoukettei.html |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=霧島市 |language=ja}} ==See also== *[[List of Historic Sites of Japan (Kagoshima)]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons category|Kagoshima-jingu|Kagoshima Shrine}} * {{OSM|n|4459864389}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[category:Pages that used to use Authority control]][[en:Kagoshima Jingu]] [[category:Beppyo shrines]] [[category:Shinto shrines in Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[en:Kagoshima Jingu]][[category:Shikinai Taisha]] [[category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[category:History of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[category:Ōsumi Province]] [[category:Ichinomiya]] [[category:Important Cultural Properties of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[category:Kagoshima prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[category:Kirishima, Kagoshima]] [[category:Jingū]] [[category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 7]] [[category:confused probably misplaced articles linked from page Torinoichi probably under wrong names recheck that page and its outlinks later]] [[category:kk]] [[category:attempting to force efresh]] [[category:bump1-19]] [[category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]][[category:Kagoshima Jingu]][[category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[category:refreshing imports]] [[category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]][[category:Kagoshima Jingu]][[category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:qq]][[en:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:qq]] [[en:Kagoshima Shrine]]

The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. [[Emperor Ōjin]]
[[Empress Jingū]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 2496, Hayato-chō Uchi, Kirishima-shi, Kagoshima-ken 899-5116 | website = | architecture_style = [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''irimoya-zukuri'']] | festival = August 15 (lunar) | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Kagoshima Shrine'''|鹿児島神宮|''Kagoshima-jingū''}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the [[Hayato, Kagoshima|Hayatomachi-uchi]] neighborhood of the city of [[Kirishima, Kagoshima|Kirishima]], [[Kagoshima prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Ōsumi Province]]. The main festival of the shrine are held annually on August 15 by the [[lunar calendar]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Historically it was also known by the names {{nihongo| '''Ōsumi Shō-Hachiman-gū''' |大隅正八幡宮||}} and {{nihongo| '''Kokubu Hachiman-gū'''|国分八幡宮||}}. The shrine precincts was designated as a [[Historic Sites of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/280010|title= 大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} == Enshrined ''Kami'' == The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kagoshima-jingū are:{{Cite web |title=由緒について - 鹿児島神宮 |url=https://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=kagoshima-jingu.jp}} ; Main shrine * {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]]'''|天津日高彦火火出見尊|}}, son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyotama-hime]]'''| 豊玉比売命|}}, wife of Hoori, paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu ; Subsidiary shrines * [[Emperor Chūai]] (帯中比子尊) * [[Empress Jingū]] (息長帯比売命) - Wife of Emperor Chūai. * [[Emperor Ōjin]] (品陀和気尊) * [[Nakatsuhime]] (中比売命) - Wife of Emperor Ōjin. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, the Kagoshima Jingū during the [[Age of the Gods]], as Takachiho Palace, the residence of [[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] (彦火火出見尊), the third and youngest son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] and ancestor of [[Emperor Jimmu]]. It was moved to its current location in 708, and Setsusha Sekitai-gu (Ishitai Shrine) is currently located on the former site. Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. 鹿児島神宮 | image = Kagoshimajingu Chokushiden.JPG | caption = Imperial Messenger's Hall (ICP) {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Kagoshima Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|31|45|13.37|N|130|44|16.3|E|region:JP-46|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Kagoshima-jingū | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Hachiman]] | deity = [[Hoori]]
[[Toyotama-hime]]
[[Emperor Chūai]]
[[Emperor Ōjin]]
[[Empress Jingū]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 2496, Hayato-chō Uchi, Kirishima-shi, Kagoshima-ken 899-5116 | website = | architecture_style = [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''irimoya-zukuri'']] | festival = August 15 (lunar) | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Kagoshima Shrine'''|鹿児島神宮|''Kagoshima-jingū''}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the [[Hayato, Kagoshima|Hayatomachi-uchi]] neighborhood of the city of [[Kirishima, Kagoshima|Kirishima]], [[Kagoshima prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Ōsumi Province]]. The main festival of the shrine are held annually on August 15 by the [[lunar calendar]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Historically it was also known by the names {{nihongo| '''Ōsumi Shō-Hachiman-gū''' |大隅正八幡宮||}} and {{nihongo| '''Kokubu Hachiman-gū'''|国分八幡宮||}}. The shrine precincts was designated as a [[Historic Sites of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/280010|title= 大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} == Enshrined ''Kami'' == The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kagoshima-jingū are:{{Cite web |title=由緒について - 鹿児島神宮 |url=https://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=kagoshima-jingu.jp}} ; Main shrine * {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]]'''|天津日高彦火火出見尊|}}, son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyotama-hime]]'''| 豊玉比売命|}}, wife of Hoori, paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu ; Subsidiary shrines * [[Emperor Chūai]] (帯中比子尊) * [[Empress Jingū]] (息長帯比売命) - Wife of Emperor Chūai. * [[Emperor Ōjin]] (品陀和気尊) * [[Nakatsuhime]] (中比売命) - Wife of Emperor Ōjin. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, the Kagoshima Jingū during the [[Age of the Gods]], as Takachiho Palace, the residence of [[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] (彦火火出見尊), the third and youngest son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] and ancestor of [[Emperor Jimmu]]. It was moved to its current location in 708, and Setsusha Sekitai-gu (Ishitai Shrine) is currently located on the former site. Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. Kagoshima-jingu, honden.jpg|Honden (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Auxiliary Auxiliary-Shrine Shisyo-jinja 001.jpg|Shisho Jinja (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Decoration of Shrine Buildings 001.jpg|Decoration on Chokushi-den (ICP) ===National Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿|Main Shrine}}, {{nihongo|'''Chokushi-den'''|勅使殿|Imperial Messenger Hall}}, and {{nihongo|'''Sessha Shisho Jinja Honden'''|摂社四所神社本殿|Sub-shrine Shisho Jinja Main Shrine}}, constructed in 1755 by Shimazu Shigetoshi and completed by Shimazu Shigehide. Designated [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]] in 2022{{Cite web |last=霧島市 |title=国宝・重要文化財(建造物)の指定について |url=http://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kokuhoukettei.html |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=霧島市 |language=ja}} ==See also== *[[List of Historic Sites of Japan (Kagoshima)]] *[[Ichinomiya]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category|Kagoshima-jingu|Kagoshima Shrine}} * {{OSM|n|4459864389}} {{Shinto shrine}} [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]][[en:Kagoshima Jingu]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[en:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:Shikinai Taisha]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:History of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Ōsumi Province]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Kagoshima Prefecture]] [[Category:Kagoshima prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[Category:Kirishima, Kagoshima]] [[Category:Jingū]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 7]] [[Category:confused probably misplaced articles linked from page Torinoichi probably under wrong names recheck that page and its outlinks later]] [[Category:kk]] [[Category:attempting to force efresh]] [[Category:bump1-19]] [[Category:refreshing categories imported on 2024-01-19]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]][[Category:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[Category:refreshing imports]] [[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]][[Category:Kagoshima Jingu]][[Category:second attempt at refreshing on January 27 2024]] [[en:Kagoshima Jingu]][[en:Kagoshima Jingu]][[en:Kagoshima Shrine]] {{Beppyo Shrines}}

The shrine precincts was designated as a [[Historic Sites of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/280010|title= 大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} == Enshrined ''Kami'' == The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kagoshima-jingū are:{{Cite web |title=由緒について - 鹿児島神宮 |url=https://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=kagoshima-jingu.jp}} ; Main shrine * {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]]'''|天津日高彦火火出見尊|}}, son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyotama-hime]]'''| 豊玉比売命|}}, wife of Hoori, paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu ; Subsidiary shrines * [[Emperor Chūai]] (帯中比子尊) * [[Empress Jingū]] (息長帯比売命) - Wife of Emperor Chūai. * [[Emperor Ōjin]] (品陀和気尊) * [[Nakatsuhime]] (中比売命) - Wife of Emperor Ōjin. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, the Kagoshima Jingū during the [[Age of the Gods]], as Takachiho Palace, the residence of [[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] (彦火火出見尊), the third and youngest son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] and ancestor of [[Emperor Jimmu]]. It was moved to its current location in 708, and Setsusha Sekitai-gu (Ishitai Shrine) is currently located on the former site. Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. The main festival of the shrine are held annually on August 15 by the [[lunar calendar]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Historically it was also known by the names {{nihongo| '''Ōsumi Shō-Hachiman-gū''' |大隅正八幡宮||}} and {{nihongo| '''Kokubu Hachiman-gū'''|国分八幡宮||}}. The shrine precincts was designated as a [[Historic Sites of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/280010|title= 大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} == Enshrined ''Kami'' == The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kagoshima-jingū are:{{Cite web |title=由緒について - 鹿児島神宮 |url=https://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=kagoshima-jingu.jp}} ; Main shrine * {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]]'''|天津日高彦火火出見尊|}}, son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyotama-hime]]'''| 豊玉比売命|}}, wife of Hoori, paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu ; Subsidiary shrines * [[Emperor Chūai]] (帯中比子尊) * [[Empress Jingū]] (息長帯比売命) - Wife of Emperor Chūai. * [[Emperor Ōjin]] (品陀和気尊) * [[Nakatsuhime]] (中比売命) - Wife of Emperor Ōjin. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, the Kagoshima Jingū during the [[Age of the Gods]], as Takachiho Palace, the residence of [[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] (彦火火出見尊), the third and youngest son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] and ancestor of [[Emperor Jimmu]]. It was moved to its current location in 708, and Setsusha Sekitai-gu (Ishitai Shrine) is currently located on the former site. Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. [[Toyotama-hime]]
[[Emperor Chūai]]
[[Emperor Ōjin]]
[[Empress Jingū]] | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 2496, Hayato-chō Uchi, Kirishima-shi, Kagoshima-ken 899-5116 | website = | architecture_style = [[East Asian hip-and-gable roof|''irimoya-zukuri'']] | festival = August 15 (lunar) | leadership = | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|[[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Property]]}} }} {{nihongo|'''Kagoshima Shrine'''|鹿児島神宮|''Kagoshima-jingū''}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in the [[Hayato, Kagoshima|Hayatomachi-uchi]] neighborhood of the city of [[Kirishima, Kagoshima|Kirishima]], [[Kagoshima prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former [[Ōsumi Province]]. The main festival of the shrine are held annually on August 15 by the [[lunar calendar]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} Historically it was also known by the names {{nihongo| '''Ōsumi Shō-Hachiman-gū''' |大隅正八幡宮||}} and {{nihongo| '''Kokubu Hachiman-gū'''|国分八幡宮||}}. The shrine precincts was designated as a [[Historic Sites of Japan|National Historic Site]] in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/280010|title= 大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=August 20, 2020}} == Enshrined ''Kami'' == The ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kagoshima-jingū are:{{Cite web |title=由緒について - 鹿児島神宮 |url=https://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=kagoshima-jingu.jp}} ; Main shrine * {{nihongo|'''[[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]]'''|天津日高彦火火出見尊|}}, son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyotama-hime]]'''| 豊玉比売命|}}, wife of Hoori, paternal grandmother of Emperor Jimmu ; Subsidiary shrines * [[Emperor Chūai]] (帯中比子尊) * [[Empress Jingū]] (息長帯比売命) - Wife of Emperor Chūai. * [[Emperor Ōjin]] (品陀和気尊) * [[Nakatsuhime]] (中比売命) - Wife of Emperor Ōjin. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, the Kagoshima Jingū during the [[Age of the Gods]], as Takachiho Palace, the residence of [[Hoori|Hikohohodemi no Mikoto]] (彦火火出見尊), the third and youngest son of [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto]] and [[Konohanasakuya-hime]] and ancestor of [[Emperor Jimmu]]. It was moved to its current location in 708, and Setsusha Sekitai-gu (Ishitai Shrine) is currently located on the former site. Takaya-no-yamanoe ''misasagi'', said to be the mausoleum of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, is located 13 kilometers northwest of the shrine. It is also said that this former shrine is where the [[Hachiman]] deity appeared in the fifth year of [[Emperor Kinmei]]'s reign (544), which is why the shrine was called the Sho-Hachiman-gū, or "true Hachiman shrine". Per the ''Hachiman Godokun'' (八幡愚童訓), when Ōhirume, the daughter of the great king of [[Chen dynasty|Chen]], was seven years old, the light of the morning sun pierced her chest, and she became pregnant. The prince was born, and the royal subjects, suspicious of him, put him on an empty ship and set it afloat on the ocean, hoping to claim the area where the ship was located as their territory. The prince landed in Ōsumi and was named "Hachiman" by [[Emperor Keitai]], although some other accounts state that the princess was on the ship, and gave birth after his arrived in Ōsumi.{{Cite web |title=神社啓蒙 7巻目録1巻. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times. Kagoshima-jingu, honden.jpg|Honden (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Auxiliary Auxiliary-Shrine Shisyo-jinja 001.jpg|Shisho Jinja (ICP) Kagoshima-jingu Decoration of Shrine Buildings 001.jpg|Decoration on Chokushi-den (ICP) ===National Important Cultural Properties=== *{{nihongo|'''Honden'''|本殿|Main Shrine}}, {{nihongo|'''Chokushi-den'''|勅使殿|Imperial Messenger Hall}}, and {{nihongo|'''Sessha Shisho Jinja Honden'''|摂社四所神社本殿|Sub-shrine Shisho Jinja Main Shrine}}, constructed in 1755 by Shimazu Shigetoshi and completed by Shimazu Shigehide. [5] - 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2556086 |access-date=2022-09-28 |website=dl.ndl.go.jp |language=ja}} Per the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'', Hachiman later relocated to [[Usa, Oita|Usa]] and eventually to [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu]]. For centuries there was a rivalry between [[Usa Shrine|Usa Hachimangū]] and Kagoshima Jingū over which one had the legitimate deity, and Usa Hachimangū secretly sent messengers to Kagoshima sent 15 (or even 14) messengers to burn down Kagoshima Jingū. As that happened, the character for "Shō-Hachiman(正八幡)" appeared in the black smoke rising from the burning shrine. These messengers were so frightened that they fled to [[Mizobe, Kagoshima|Mizobe]], where they were punished by the gods and 13 died one after another. The local people then took pity on those who had died, and built mounds at the places where they had fallen. These mounds are located in the northern part of the Kokubu Plain. The Jusanzukabara (Thirteen Mounds) Historic Site Park derives its name from this legend and is located in the northeastern part of the area, near [[Kagoshima Airport]]. The first mention of the shrine in reliable historical records is in the [[Engishiki]], compiled during the reign of [[Emperor Daigo]], which lists it as the only ''Shikinai Taisha'' in southern Kyushu (Hyuga, Osumi, and Satsuma). During the [[Kenkyū]] era (1190 - 1199), the shrine's territory was over 2,500 [[Japanese units of measurement#area|chō]], and it held estates with 1,000 ''[[koku]]'' until the end of the [[Edo period]].{{Cite web |title=鹿児島神宮 {{!}} 鹿児島県神社庁 |url=https://www.kagojinjacho.or.jp/tanbou/28/ |access-date=2022-09-29 |website=www.kagojinjacho.or.jp}} The shrine was patronized by the [[Shimazu clan]] of [[Satsuma Domain]] from the [[Sengoku period]]. In 1871, under the [[Meiji government]]'s [[State Shinto]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ranked Shinto shrines]], the Kagoshima Jingū was initially ranked as an {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd rank|国幣中社|Kokuhei Chūsha}}. It was promoted to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 2nd rank|官幣中社|Kanpei Chūsha}} in 1874 and to a {{nihongo|Imperial shrine, 1st rank|官幣大社|Kanpei Taisha}} in 1895. After the war, the shrine became a part of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]].{{cite book |last1=Isomura |first1=Yukio |last2=Sakai |first2=Hideya |title=(国指定史跡事典) National Historic Site Encyclopedia |date=2012 |publisher=学生社 |isbn=4311750404}}{{in lang|ja}} [[Archaeological excavation]]s have been carried out since 1994. Within the current precincts a large number of shards of Chinese and Thai ceramics from the 14th to the first half of the 15th century have been found, indicating that the shrine was involved in overseas trade with mainland Asia from the [[Kamakura period]] to the [[Muromachi period]]. The National Historic Site designation also includes the sites of four houses of the hereditary priesthood of the shrine. Each of these sites was a fortified mansion, with wide and deep moats and earthen ramparts. Ceramic shards from China and Southeast Asia have also been found in each of these locations, which were inhabited continuously from the mid-[[Heian period]] into modern times.
