It is classified as a Shikinai Taisha (a shrine of the highest Rank according to the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932|lt=Kanpei Taisha}}), and is the Ichinomiya of {{ill|Ōsumi Province|en|Ōsumi Province|qid=Q981002|lt=Ōsumi Province}}. Its former Ranking under the modern shrine Ranking system was as a Kanpei Taisha, and today it is one of the {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|qid=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. In earlier times it was also known as “{{ill|Kagoshima Jingū|ja|大隅正八幡宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daosumi Seihachiman Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 鹿児島神宮|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q704695}}” and “{{ill|Kokubu-Hachimangu|ja|国府八幡宮|qid=Q11420856}}.” == Deities == The enshrined deities are as follows[http://kagoshima-jingu.jp/yuisyo.php "About the History"] (Official website).: ; Principal Deities :* '''{{ill|Hoori|en|Hoori|qid=Q1051960|lt=Amatsuhidaka Hikohohide-mikoto}}''' (also known as Yamayukihiko) :* '''{{ill|Toyotama-hime|en|Toyotama-hime|qid=Q2329261|lt=Toyotamahime-mikoto}}''' – the consort (後神) of Hoori. ; Associated Deities (Sodaten-shin) :* {{ill|Emperor Chūai|ar|الإمبراطور تشواي|arz|الامبراطور تشواى|azb|چوای (ایمپیراتور)|ca|Chūai|cs|Čúai|de|Chūai|es|Chūai Tennō|fa|امپراتور چوآی|fr|Chūai|hr|Chūai|hu|Csúai japán császár|id|Kaisar Chūai|it|Chūai|ja|仲哀天皇|ka|ტიუაი|ko|주아이 천황|nl|Chuai|pl|Chūai|pt|Chuai|ru|Император Тюай|sh|Car Chūai|simple|Emperor Chūai|sl|Cesar Čuaj|sv|Chuai|th|จักรพรรดิชูไอ|tl|Emperador Chūai|tr|Chūai (imparator)|uk|Імператор Тюай|uz|Imperator Chūai|vi|Thiên hoàng Chūai|zh|仲哀天皇|zh_min_nan|Tyûai Thian-hông|zh_yue|仲哀天皇|qid=Q179971|lt=Obi Chūhiko-mikoto}} :* {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Okinaga Ta-hime-mikoto}} – the consort of Emperor Chūai. :* {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|qid=Q317997|lt=Homudawake-mikoto}} (the 15th Emperor Ōjin, also revered as Hachiman Ōkami) :* {{ill|Nakatsuhime|fa|ناکاتسو هیمه|ja|仲姫命|zh|仲姬命|qid=Q11378496|lt=Nakahime-mikoto}} : The four associated deities are enshrined together in connection with Hachiman. == History == According to the shrine’s tradition, its foundation dates back either to the distant {{ill|Age of the gods (Japanese mythology)|ja|神代|qid=Q3577055}} or “to the time of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu}}, when the palace at Takachiho – the residence of {{ill|Hoori|en|Hoori|qid=Q1051960|lt=Amatsuhidaka Hikohohide-mikoto}} – was established as a shrine.” In Wadō 1 (708), the shrine was relocated to its present site; at the old shrine site now stands a subsidiary shrine, Ishitai Shrine ({{ill|Ishitai Shrine|ja|石體神社}}). Approximately 13 km to the northwest lies Takayama Jōryō, reputedly the imperial tomb of {{ill|Hoori|en|Hoori|qid=Q1051960|lt=Amatsuhidaka Hikohohide-mikoto}}. It is also said that in the 5th year of {{ill|Emperor Kinmei|en|Emperor Kinmei|qid=Q329792|lt=Emperor Kinmei}} (544) the deity {{ill|Hachiman|en|Hachiman|qid=Q261637|lt=Hachiman}} manifested at the old shrine site. The reason the shrine is also called “Seihachiman” is explained in the ''Hachiman Gudōkun'', which states: ::: “In the land of Shindan (as seen from India, i.e. China), the daughter of the great king, Obiru-onna, when she was seven, was pierced in the chest by the light of the morning sun and became pregnant, giving birth to a prince. The ministers, finding this strange, set her adrift on a ship, decreeing that the place where the ship came to moor would be their territory. The ship eventually reached the rocky shores of Osumi, and the prince was named Hachiman.” ::: (In another account, as recorded in ''Shinshakēmō'' by {{ill|Shiroi Sōin|ja|白井宗因}}, the figure is called “King Chin” and the daughter is named Hachiman.) It is recorded in the ''Konjaku Monogatari-shū'' that Hachiman appeared in {{ill|Ōsumi Province|en|Ōsumi Province|qid=Q981002|lt=Ōsumi Province}}, then moved to Usa Shrine ({{ill|Usa Jingū|de|Usa Hachiman-gū|el|Ούσα Τζίνγκου|eu|Usa jingū|fr|Usa Hachiman-gū|id|Kuil Usa|ja|宇佐神宮|ko|우사 신궁|la|Usa-jingū|or|ଉସାଜିଙ୍ଗୁ|ru|Уса-дзингу|simple|Usa Jingū|tok|tomo sewi suli Usa|tr|Usa Jingū|zh|宇佐神宮|qid=Q715632}}), and finally left its mark at Iwashimizu Hachimangū ({{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|en|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|qid=Q710098|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}}). As the character “正” (sei) in “Daosumi Seihachiman” indicates, Kagoshima Jingu is regarded as the head shrine of the Hachiman shrines. According to tradition, there was once a dispute between Kokubu Hachiman and Usa Hachiman over which was the legitimate Hachiman. Usa Hachiman is said to have secretly sent 15 envoys (or 14, according to some accounts) to set fire to Kokubu Hachiman. In the midst of the billowing black smoke rising from the burning shrine, the characters “正八幡” appeared; the envoys, terrified by this sight, fled to Mizobata, but were struck down one after another until only 13 remained. Later, the local people, moved with pity for those who had died, built Kofuns at each site where an envoy fell; because there were 13 such mounds, the place came to be known as {{ill|Q11404752|ja|十三塚原|qid=Q11404752}}. This site lies to the north of the Kokubu Plain in {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|qid=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, and its northeastern area is home to Kagoshima Airport and a historic park based on this tradition. There are several other traditions concerning the envoys of Usa Hachiman that differ in detail from the above. The earliest reliable record is found in the ''Engishiki Jinmyōchō'', compiled during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Daigo|en|Emperor Daigo|qid=Q329753|lt=Emperor Daigo}}, which lists the shrine as “Kagoshima Jinja, Ōsumi Province, Kuwahara District.” In southern Kyushu (Hyūga, Osumi, and Satsuma), it is the only Shikinai Taisha (i.e. the only Kanpei Taisha) of the highest Rank. Owing to its exalted status, it produced many prominent local figures – such as members of the Kuwabata and Zeisho clans – among its shrine officials. During the Heian period, when Usa Hachiman enshrined branch Hachiman shrines in the five regions of Kyushu, Hachiman was also enshrined here. Since then the shrine has also been known as Seihachiman-gū, Daosumi Seihachiman-gū, and Kokubu Hachiman-gū. In the Kenkyū era (1190–1199), the shrine’s territory covered over 2,500 chō, and by the end of the Edo period it had an income of about 1,000 koku. In Daiei 7 (1527), the shrine was burned down by warfare. In Tenmon 20 (1551), with the consent of the later Nara Emperor, Shimazu Takahisa ordered the monk {{ill|Nichi-shu|ja|日秀上人}} (of the Shingon sect) to restore the shrine, and on December 13, Eiroku 3 (1560) it was relocated to a new shrine building. From the Sengoku period through the Edo period, the shrine was revered by the local daimyō, the {{ill|Shimazu clan|en|Shimazu clan|qid=Q1061406|lt=Shimazu clan}}. In 1871 (Meiji 4), under the modern shrine Ranking system established by the Meiji government, it was classified as a national mid-Rank shrine ({{ill|Kokuhei Chūsha|ja|国幣中社}}) under the name “Kagoshima Jinja.” In 1874 (Meiji 7) it was granted the title “Jingū” and, under the modern system, was classified as a national mid-Rank shrine ({{ill|Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|ja|官幣中社|lt=Kanpei Chūsha}}); in 1895 (Meiji 28) it was elevated to a national high shrine ({{ill|Kanpei Taisha (disambiguation)|ja|官幣大社|zh|官幣大社|qid=Q10209769}}). After World War II it became one of the {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|qid=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. On November 10, 1935 (Showa 10), while participating in an Army Special Exercise, Emperor Shōwa made an official visit{{Cite book |和書|author=原武史 |title=昭和天皇御召列車全記録 |publisher=新潮社 |year=2016-09-30 |page=77 |isbn=978-4-10-320523-4}}. On November 19, 2021 (Reiwa 3), the National Cultural Council recommended that the main hall, worship hall, Chokushi-den, and the main halls of the four subsidiary shrines be designated as Important Cultural Properties{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kokuho-jubun.html |title=Regarding the Designation of National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties (Structures) |publisher=Kirishima City |date=2021-10-29 |accessdate=2022-02-11}}. The following day, as announced in the Official Gazette dated February 9, 2022 (Reiwa 4), they were formally designated as Important Cultural Properties{{cite news|title=Kirishima Jingū Officially Designated as a National Treasure; Kagoshima Jingu Also Named an Important Cultural Property|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220209055427/https://www3.nhk.or.jp/lnews/kagoshima/20220209/5050017814.html |publisher=NHK NEWS WEB |date=2022-02-09 |accessdate=2022-02-11}}{{Cite web|和書|date=2022-02-09 |url=http://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kokuhoukettei.html |title=Regarding the Designation of National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties (Structures) |publisher=Kirishima City |accessdate=2022-02-11}}. == Grounds == [[File:Sangoku meisho zue Kagoshima Shrine.jpg|thumb|450x450px|Samune image (Edo-period Kagoshima Jingu from ''Sangoku Meisho Zue'').]] * Great Torii – a torii spanning a public road * Dedicated Wooden Horse – a divine (wooden) horse dedicated in Shōwa 18According to the on-site information board. * Divine Horse Stable * Temizuya * Main Hall, Worship Hall, and Chokushi-den – Designated as Important Cultural Properties. The shrine buildings, originally constructed in Keichō 6 (1601), later suffered severe termite damage; they were rebuilt beginning in Hōreki 5 (1755) through a donation by Shimazu Shigenoshi and were completed the following year during Shimazu Shigehiro’s era{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kyoiku/rekishi/bunkazai/shitebunkazai/bunka-hayato.html#5 |title=Main Hall, Worship Hall, Chokushi-den, and Main Halls of the Four Subsidiary Shrines of Kagoshima Jingu |access-date=2022-07-12 |publisher=Kirishima City Office, Education and Cultural Affairs Group}}. The Chokushi-den, which functions as the entrance to the shrine compound, stands alongside the Worship Hall and Main Hall on the north side. All buildings are richly decorated—the Chokushi-den features a depiction of a dragon being borne, the Worship Hall has a ceiling painting, and the Main Hall, extremely large in scale, is adorned throughout with sculptures and wall paintings by the Satsuma artist Kimura Tantetsu, finished in vivid colors and lacquer, with dragon carvings entwined around its front-facing columns{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.pref.kagoshima.jp/ba08/documents/62592_20220210110955-1.pdf |title=Main Hall, Worship Hall, Chokushi-den, and Main Halls of the Four Subsidiary Shrines of Kagoshima Jingu |access-date=2022-07-12 |publisher=Kagoshima Prefecture |format=PDF}}. * Stone Lantern from the Rebuilding of the Main Shrine – a prefecturally designated tangible cultural property. Donated to the main shrine (current Kagoshima Jingu) in Hōreki 6 (1756), this two-legged stone lantern is known as the “Koto-bashira Lantern.” An inscription regarding the construction of the shrine buildings is carved on the front of its base{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kyoiku/rekishi/bunkazai/shitebunkazai/bunka-hayato.html#32 |title=Stone Lantern from the Rebuilding of the Main Shrine |access-date=2022-07-12 |publisher=Kirishima City Office, Education and Cultural Affairs Group}}. * Shinden (Sacred Field) * Sacred Tree – said to have been planted during the {{ill|Kenkyū Period|ja|建久年間}} and reputed to be about 800 years old. * Tortoise Stone * Hayato Historical and Folklore Museum – This facility comprises history and folklore exhibition rooms as well as a Japanese-style room. It exhibits documents related to Kagoshima Jingu, archaeological materials (such as earthenware and stone axes) excavated from Hayato, as well as materials and folk implements related to local performing arts (including the bell-ringing horse dance). Its Japanese-style room recreates a Showa-era atmosphere{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/shisetsu/kyoiku/028.html |title=Hayato Historical and Folklore Museum |access-date=2022-07-12 |publisher=Kirishima City Office}}. * Shrine Office * Yōseikan === Subsidiary and Associated Shrines === * Shishō Jinja – Designated as an Important Cultural Property. Deities enshrined: {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|ar|الإمبراطور نينتوكو|arz|الامبراطور نينتوكو|azb|نینتوکو (ایمپیراتور)|bn|সম্রাট নিন্তকু|br|Impalaer Nintoku|ca|Emperador Nintoku|cs|Nintoku|de|Nintoku|es|Nintoku Tennō|fa|امپراتور نینتوکو|fi|Nintoku|fr|Nintoku|hr|Nintoku|hu|Nintoku japán császár|id|Kaisar Nintoku|it|Nintoku|ja|仁徳天皇|ka|ნინტოკუ|ko|닌토쿠 천황|lt|Imperatorius Nintoku|ms|Maharaja Nintoku|nds|Nintoku|nl|Nintoku|pl|Nintoku|pt|Nintoku|ru|Император Нинтоку|sh|Car Nintoku|simple|Emperor Nintoku|sl|Cesar Nintoku|sv|Nintoku|th|จักรพรรดินินโตกุ|tl|Emperador Nintoku|tr|Nintoku (imparator)|uk|Імператор Нінтоку|uz|Imperator Nintoku|vi|Thiên hoàng Nintoku|yo|Emperor Nintoku|zh|仁德天皇|zh_min_nan|Nintoku Thian-hông|zh_yue|仁德天皇|qid=Q313119|lt=Great Sparrow-mikoto}}, {{ill|Princess Ishi-hime|en|Princess Ishi-hime|qid=Q11585498|lt=Ishihime-mikoto}}, Arata Waro-onna, and Ne-tori-mikoto. Its annual festival is held on November 15. * Takeuchi Jinja – Enshrines the deity {{ill|Takenouchi no Sukune|en|Takenouchi no Sukune|qid=Q1073668|lt=Takenouchi no Sukune}}. * Hayabusa Jinja – Enshrines the deity {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}}. * Sannoshi – Three shrines are built in front of the entrance torii. * Gomon Jinja – Two shrines are built at the foot of the stone steps leading into the grounds. * Ame-no-sha – Enshrines the deity {{ill|Watatsumi|en|Watatsumi|qid=Q1474187|lt=Toyotamahiko-mikoto}}; its example festival is held on October 11. * Shōkon Jinja * Inari Jinja * Yamajin Jinja * Otarachinome Jinja * Takachiho Palace Ruins / Ishitai Shrine – The former main shrine; the site where the main hall of Takachiho Palace once stood. * Hoshoku Jinja == Gallery == File:Kagoshima-jingu, shaden.jpg|Shrine Buildings

Designated on February 9, 2022 (Reiwa 4)Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Notification No. 10, February 9, Reiwa 4.[https://www.city-kirishima.jp/bunka/kyoiku/rekishi/bunkazai/shitebunkazai/bunka-hayato.html#5 Cultural Properties [Hayato]] (Kirishima City website, updated February 8, 2022). ** Main Hall and Worship Hall ** Chokushi-den ** Main halls of the four subsidiary shrines * Helmet with Konito-Iwa Armor and Attached Large Sleeve (Crafts) : Donated by Kabayama Yukihisa, a senior retainer of the Shimazu family. Designated on March 31, 1953 (Shōwa 28){{国指定文化財等データベース|201|5547|紺絲威鎧〈兜、大袖付／〉}} * Helmet with Iroiro-I Doromaru Armor and Attached Large Sleeve (Crafts) : Donated by Shimazu Takahisa in Genroku 1 (1558). Held by the Kagoshima Prefecture Historical Materials Center Reimei-kan. Designated on March 31, 1953 (Shōwa 28){{国指定文化財等データベース|201|5548|色々威胴丸〈兜、大袖付／〉}} * Helmet with Iroiro-I Doromaru Armor and Attached Large Sleeve (Crafts) : Donated by Shimazu Takahisa in Genroku 1 (1558). Currently held by the Tokyo National Museum. Designated on March 31, 1953 (Shōwa 28){{国指定文化財等データベース|201|5549|色々威胴丸〈兜、大袖付／〉}} * Sword, Unsigned (Densokuju) (Crafts) : Although its whereabouts became unknown after seizure by the occupation forces following the war, a sword matching its distinctive characteristics was discovered in Australia in 2022 (Reiwa 4){{cite news|title=Old National Treasure Sword Possibly Discovered in Australia After Being Seized by GHQ Post-War|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220223195910/https://www3.nhk.or.jp/news/html/20220224/k10013498361000.html |publisher=NHK NEWS WEB |date=2022-02-24 |accessdate=2022-03-03}}. Designated on April 8, 1918 (Taishō 7){{国指定文化財等データベース|201|10468|刀〈無銘（伝則重）／〉}}. * Sword, Inscribed “Sōjū-sumi Aki Hiro, Meitoku San” (Crafts) : Made in Meitoku 3 (1392); donated by the 27th head of the Shimazu family, Shimazu Sayo. Although it was lost following postwar occupation seizures, it was rediscovered at auction and repurchased by the shrine in 2003 (Heisei 15). It is now housed at the Kagoshima Prefecture Historical Materials Center Reimei-kan. Designated on April 25, 1927 (Shōwa 2){{国指定文化財等データベース|201|10469|刀〈銘相州住秋広／明徳三〉}} === National Historic Sites === * The grounds of Daosumi Seihachiman Shrine and the site of the clan residence – designated on October 17, 2013 (Heisei 25){{国指定文化財等データベース|401|00003825|大隅正八幡宮境内及び社家跡}} === National Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Properties[Measures to create records for intangible folk cultural properties] === * [[Hatsu Uma Sai (Kagoshima Jingu)|Satsuma Horse Dance Custom]] – Selected on February 12, 2002 (Heisei 14){{Cite web|和書|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/312/753 |title=Satsuma Horse Dance Custom / Measures for Record-making for Intangible Folk Cultural Properties |access-date=2022-07-12 |publisher=National Cultural Properties Database / Agency for Cultural Affairs}} === Kagoshima Prefecture–designated Cultural Properties === * Tangible Cultural Properties ** Stone lantern from the rebuilding of the main shrine (Structure) **: Designated on April 22, 2014 (Heisei 26) ** Ceramic ware owned by Kagoshima Jingu (Crafts) **: On March 25, 2008 (Heisei 20), it was designated as “Kagoshima Jingu Treasures: Ceramic Ware” by Kirishima City as a designated tangible cultural property (Crafts), and on April 23, 2010 it was designated as a Kagoshima Prefecture Cultural Property ** Kagoshima Jingu Documents (Ancient Documents) **: Includes various appointment documents related to the shrine such as the Shichihachiman Shrine priestess appointment documents and inscriptions on official letters;
